name: Grand Tourbillon
description: Grand Tourbillon is an immense gas giant whose atmospheric bands rotate at different speeds, creating a layered, spinning visual effect reminiscent of the tourbillon mechanism in ancient timepieces. The upper atmosphere is banded in cream, amber, and deep burgundy, with storm systems that trace elegant spiraling paths between the counter-rotating layers. Two suns illuminate the planet from different angles, casting complex shadow patterns through the cloud layers and creating a perpetual display of shifting light and color.

Descending into Grand Tourbillon's atmosphere is like sinking into a slowly churning machine of gas and pressure. The upper layers are cold and thin, whistling with high-altitude winds, while the deeper bands generate crushing pressures and temperatures that rise toward the planet's hidden core. The storms are colossal, their lightning visible from orbit as flickering webs that illuminate cloud formations the size of terrestrial worlds. Microbial life floats in the temperate middle layers, vast colonial organisms that drift on thermal currents and glow faintly with metabolic bioluminescence.

A derelict space station orbits at the edge of Grand Tourbillon's ring system, its design unlike any known spacefaring culture. The station appears to have been an atmospheric research platform, its instruments still pointed at the gas giant's banded layers. A repeating signal from deep within the planet's atmosphere was the station's apparent focus, a structured transmission that originates from below the depth at which any probe has survived. The signal's complexity suggests either an unknown natural phenomenon or a transmitter embedded impossibly deep within the gas giant.

Grand Tourbillon's helium-3 reserves and trace antimatter in the upper atmosphere make it a fuel harvesting station of immense potential, and several corporations maintain skimming operations in the outer bands. The derelict station's technology, though damaged, has yielded advances in atmospheric shielding that have yet to be fully replicated. The deep signal has become the subject of a quiet competition among research institutions, each attempting to develop probes capable of reaching its source, a depth where pressures could compress hydrogen into metallic form and where something continues to broadcast with clockwork regularity.
